THE FOUNDATIONS — what it takes to verify one pin

The top trust tier of this atlas is formal (Lean) verification, and the experiment was to formalize the bribery paper behind the town. The finding is that “formalize the paper” is the wrong unit of work: what actually has to be built is the theory the paper — and half of computational social choice — stands on. Exact rational LP duality and the ellipsoid method (a large chunk of Grötschel–Lovász–Schrijver), a real machine model in which “polynomial time” is a theorem about Turing machines rather than a slogan, and the parameterized-complexity basics (what an FPT reduction is, hardness of Clique) that the Handbook's hardness results silently assume. None of this existed in mathlib. The chart below is that theory, partially built — and it is a reusable foundation for every future pin, not a per-paper cost.

External results enter as explicitly stated assumptions (Lean interfaces — never axioms), so a paper can be verified modulo named citations: “†” below marks these. That packaging is what makes paper-scale verification feasible at all, and it is also the sharpest danger: mis-formalize an assumption and everything above it silently rests on a falsehood. This is not hypothetical — the machine audit of this very development flagged the GLS vertex-encoding interface as likely false as stated (a \(10E^2\) bit bound where Cramer-rule arithmetic forces roughly \(E^3\)), and found a legacy layer in which P = NP was a structure field, so theorems “concluding” it concluded nothing. Both were caught by auditing the assumption surface — the discipline this page exists to display.

Metrics regenerate from the repository via tools/lean_audit.py (tripwire greps, import-cone analysis, watchlist diffs) as the formalization progresses; the module structure and assumption audit are from the machine inventory of the development. 223 regression files pin proved statements to their intended shape, and an axiom-audit file re-checks every central declaration on each build.

What this is

Most of computational social choice studies finite societies: a list of voters, an integer program, an NP-hardness proof. Nearly every such result has an unexamined continuous mirror: replace the population by a distribution of voter types with masses, keep the computational question. Sometimes the mirror is easier — the integer program relaxes to a linear program and NP-hardness drops to P. Nobody has charted where. This atlas is the chart, and it is being drawn by an automated pipeline.

How a pin gets its colour

Each paper of the pilot corpus is read by an adversarial triple (proponent, opponent, judge — GPT-5.6 class models). A pin is green if the judge finds a named result whose continuous mirror survives the opponent's best case against it; red otherwise. For green papers, a packaging stage turns the mirror into a self-contained proof task (target chosen by fixed rules from what the discrete result asserts), a prover attempts it, and a second, independent model is prompted to BREAK the proof — an adversarial review, not a rubber stamp. A gold ring marks a new result: the prover settled the mirror and the adversarial review failed to break the proof. No human has audited these — that is the next tier, and saying so plainly is the point of the tier system.

The pipeline, stage by stage

Every element here is the output of a fixed chain of tools, each stage writing machine-readable records that the next stage — and this site — is built from:

  1. Harvest. Venue indexes from DBLP's CC0 bulk dump plus an OpenAlex citation snowball seeded by the Handbook of Computational Social Choice; every row records which source found it.
  2. Screen. A model sorts each candidate into comsoc / borderline / no from title and abstract; each verdict records the model that made it and its input basis (title-only verdicts are provisional by construction).
  3. Adversarial triple. Proponent, opponent and judge read the full text in sequence; the judge must name a specific theorem and quote it verbatim, and the quote is machine-checked against the source text — a pin with no checkable anchor does not turn green.
  4. Package → prove → review. For green papers, a packaging stage writes the continuous mirror up as a self-contained proof task, a prover (GPT-5.6 class, maximum reasoning effort) attempts it, and an independent model is prompted to break the proof. Only settled-and-survived earns a gold ring.
  5. Build. atlas_build.py renders this site from those records and nothing else. No pin, verdict, quote or proof on this site is hand-typed.

Trust tiers

machine-claimed (prover only) < adversarially reviewed (an independent model tries to break the proof and fails) < human-checked < formalized (Lean — see The Foundations). Every gold element on this site links to its full provenance — the exact task, the proof, the adversarial review. Nothing here is hand-typed except the map background and the curated grid data, which was itself extracted from the literature by an agent and struck by a human.

Honesty note

This is a growing chart, not a finished one. It currently covers 527 papers across 12 venue-years (AAAI 2022, AAAI 2023, AAAI 2024, AAAI 2025, AAMAS 2022, AAMAS 2023, AAMAS 2024, AAMAS 2025, IJCAI 2022, IJCAI 2023, IJCAI 2024, IJCAI 2025). The proofs are adversarially reviewed by machines, not checked by humans — and “verified” is a word this atlas reserves for the Lean tier. The town grid is one paper's vocabulary. The point of the atlas is not that it is finished — it is that every element you can click was produced, end to end, by a pipeline that can now be pointed at the next conference, the next cell, and the next area.

Openness & releases

Openness about the pipeline is part of the point, and it arrives in two steps. Already now, every published build of this site is stamped — see the footer — with the exact commit of the pipeline repository that produced it, and every gold element links its full provenance: the task as posed, the proof as returned, the adversarial review as it happened. The pipeline itself (code, prompts, harness) is still changing weekly and will be released in full once it settles; because the build stamps are public first, that release can be checked retroactively against every build that ever appeared here. One thing is never published: paper full texts — provenance pages quote only the specific named statements under discussion.
